questions.q: Define "structured questionnaire" and "unstructured interview" in the context of geographical field surveys. Give one example of a geographical research question suited to each.
questions.a: A structured questionnaire uses pre-determined, fixed-response questions (e.g., multiple choice, Likert scale) administered identically to all respondents — suited for "What percentage of farmers in Punjab use drip irrigation?" An unstructured interview uses open-ended, flexible questions allowing the interviewer to probe based on responses — suited for "Why do tribal communities in Bastar resist relocation from forest areas?" A wrong answer (e.g., swapping the examples) reveals confusion between quantitative breadth (questionnaire) and qualitative depth (interview) — students often think questionnaires can explore "why" deeply, but fixed responses limit probing.

questions.q: A student wants to study "spatial pattern of household waste segregation practices in a Delhi neighborhood." They plan to use a questionnaire. Explain why observation would be more appropriate, and describe what specific behaviors the observer would record.
questions.a: Questionnaires rely on self-reported behavior, which suffers from social desirability bias — residents may claim they segregate waste when they don't. Observation directly records actual behavior: the observer would note (1) whether households place wet/dry waste in separate bins at collection point, (2) timing and frequency of disposal, (3) contamination levels in bins, (4) informal dumping spots. A wrong answer (insisting questionnaire is fine) reveals failure to recognize the "say-do gap" in human geography — a critical competitive exam trap where students ignore method validity for sensitive or observable behaviors.

questions.q: Design a 5-question structured questionnaire segment to investigate "Impact of Metro Rail on commuting patterns in Bengaluru." Include: two closed-ended (one nominal, one ordinal), one open-ended, one multiple-response, and one Likert-scale question. Label each type.
questions.a:
1. Nominal (closed): "Primary mode of commute BEFORE Metro: (a) Bus (b) Two-wheeler (c) Car (d) Auto-rickshaw (e) Other"  
2. Ordinal (closed): "Current commute time compared to pre-Metro: (a) Much less (b) Slightly less (c) Same (d) Slightly more (e) Much more"  
3. Open-ended: "Describe one way Metro has changed your daily routine."  
4. Multiple-response: "Factors influencing your Metro usage (select all): (a) Cost (b) Time saving (c) Comfort (d) Connectivity (e) Safety (f) Other____"  
4. Likert (5-point): "Metro has improved my overall commuting experience: Strongly Disagree / Disagree / Neutral / Agree / Strongly Agree"  
A wrong answer (e.g., making all questions open-ended) reveals inability to match question type to data analysis needs — nominal/ordinal/Likert enable statistical analysis (chi-square, correlation) required in board practicals and CUET geography.

questions.q: Compare participant observation and non-participant observation for studying "street vendor eviction drives in Mumbai." Create a table with four rows: (i) Researcher role, (ii) Data depth, (iii) Ethical risk, (iv) Suitable research phase.
questions.a:
| Aspect | Participant Observation | Non-Participant Observation |
|---|---|---|
| Researcher role | Works alongside vendors, experiences eviction | Watches from distance, records notes/photos |
| Data depth | High — emic perspective, emotions, informal networks | Moderate — etic perspective, visible actions only |
| Ethical risk | High — deception if identity concealed; trauma exposure | Lower — transparency easier; but privacy concerns remain |
| Suitable phase | Exploratory phase — understanding lived experience | Systematic phase — mapping eviction patterns, counting affected |

A wrong answer (e.g., claiming participant observation has lower ethical risk) reveals misunderstanding of informed consent in vulnerable populations — a recurring JEE/NEET-adjacent ethics question in CUET geography case studies.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "For a study on 'groundwater depletion causes in Marathwada,' a questionnaire administered to 200 farmers is sufficient; interviews and observation are unnecessary." Provide three distinct geographical reasons.
questions.a:
The statement is flawed because:  
(1) Questionnaires cannot capture hydrogeological complexity — farmers may not know aquifer characteristics, recharge zones, or well interference; expert interviews with hydrologists and observation of well depths/rock types are essential.  
(2) Power dynamics — large landowners may dominate questionnaire responses, masking smallholder experiences; semi-structured interviews with stratified samples reveal equity issues.  
(3) Behavioral verification — observation of actual irrigation practices (crop choice, pump hours, flood vs drip) often contradicts self-reported data.  
A wrong answer (agreeing with the statement) reveals "method monism" — the competitive exam trap of treating one method as universally sufficient, ignoring triangulation (a core NCERT principle in Practical Work in Geography).

questions.q: You are designing a mixed-method field survey for "Urban heat island effect in Jaipur's walled city vs. planned colonies." Specify: (a) One observation protocol (what, where, when, how), (b) One interview guide theme for municipal officials, (c) One questionnaire item for residents, (d) How you will triangulate findings.
questions.a:
(a) Observation: Use infrared thermometer to measure surface temperatures of 50 points (roads, roofs, parks) in both areas at 14:00 and 22:00 hrs for 7 consecutive days; record land cover type, building height, vegetation cover.  
(b) Interview guide theme: "Planning interventions for heat mitigation — tree plantation drives, cool roof policies, building bylaws enforcement, budget allocation, inter-department coordination challenges."  
(c) Questionnaire item (Likert): "My neighborhood feels significantly hotter at night than 10 years ago: Strongly Disagree to Strongly Agree."  
(d) Triangulation: Correlate observed temperature differentials with resident perceptions (questionnaire) and policy gaps (interviews); use GIS overlay (node c12_geo_cbse_21_009) of temperature points, land use, and green cover.  
A poor answer (single method only) reveals inability to design integrated geographical research — a key competency in CBSE practical exams and CUET case-based questions.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Field survey methods are systematic techniques for collecting primary geographical data directly from the field, comprising three core approaches: ______ (standardized written instruments with open/closed questions), interview (face-to-face or telephonic verbal interaction with structured/semi-structured/unstructured formats), and observation (systematic watching and recording of phenomena, behaviors, or features in their natural setting — participant or non-participant).
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ in a bustling weekly market in your town — vendors shouting prices, buyers bargaining, goods arranged in patterns.
What is Field survey methods? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Field survey methods are systematic techniques for collecting primary geographical data directly from the field, comprising three core approaches: questionnaire (standardized written instruments with open/closed questions), interview (face-to-face or telephonic verbal interaction with structured/semi-structured/unstructured formats), and.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Field survey methods?
questions.a: Students believe "questionnaire = quantitative, interview = qualitative, observation = qualitative" as rigid categories.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can select and justify the appropriate field survey method (questionnaire, interview, or observation) for a given geographical research problem, design a basic instrument for each method, and identify two advantages and two limitations of each method with Indian context examples.
